query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are the primary constituents, adding a modest amount (~5–10 at%) of a refractory beta‐stabilizer (e.g., molybdenum) will induce the formation of finely dispersed, refractory intermetallic precipitates that hinder dislocation motion and thereby improve yield strength and creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the same alloy without the Mo addition.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium‐ and nickel‐primary equiatomic high-entropy alloy (with the remaining elements chosen to meet the 5–35 at% rule) that forms a predominantly single-phase solid solution with limited intrinsic precipitation strengthening.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of approximately 5–10 atomic percent molybdenum into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature service conditions (e.g., 600–1200 °C) where creep resistance and yield strength are critical for performance, with standard heat-treatment to allow controlled precipitate formation.
generation.structural_mediator: A dual-phase microstructure featuring a continuous high-entropy matrix in which fine, thermally stable Mo-rich intermetallic precipitates are dispersed.
generation.mechanism: The Mo addition acts as a beta stabilizer and promotes controlled precipitation in the matrix. These refractory precipitates serve as obstacles to dislocation glide and improve load transfer, providing both solid solution and precipitation strengthening effects at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: An alloy with the Mo intervention is predicted to show a significant relative improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance (e.g., on the order of a 20–30% increase) compared to the baseline alloy without Mo, with an acceptable balance of ductility.
generation.baseline: The original Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloy without any additional Mo.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable across alloys that satisfy the HEA compositional definition (each element 5–35 at%) and is targeted at high-temperature applications. However, Mo levels exceeding approximately 10 at% may lead to coarse precipitates and embrittlement, and the precise effective range may depend on other alloying elements and processing parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Mo concentration and heat-treatment protocol for achieving the desired fine precipitate distribution is uncertain; furthermore, the balance between improved high-temperature strength and potential loss in ductility requires experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline Ti-Ni primary HEA and another set with an additional 5–10 at% Mo. Subject both sets to identical processing and heat-treatment schedules. Perform elevated-temperature (e.g., 800°C) tensile and creep tests while characterizing the microstructure (using TEM and XRD) to confirm precipitate formation and distribution.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-containing alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than a 15% increase) in yield strength and creep resistance at elevated temperatures—or if it shows markedly reduced ductility or an adverse microstructural evolution compared to the baseline alloy—the hypothesis is falsified.

Refractory elements, including Rhenium (Re), Molybdenum (Mo), Niobium (Nb), Tantalum (Ta), and Tungsten (W) [] are very important for improving mechanical properties in advanced alloys such as Titanium alloys and Nickel-base superalloys. Generally, elements with a melting point higher than Titanium (Ti), such as Chromium (Cr), Hafnium (Hf), Osmium (Os), Ruthenium (Ru), Vanadium (V), and Zirconium (Zr) are also classified as refractory elements. In Titanium alloys, refractory elements, especially Mo and W, are all beta stabilizers and possess a strong solid solution strengthening characteristic []. Nb forms Ni3Nb γ phase in Nickel-base superalloys such as Inconel 718 []. The improved creep resistance of the sixth generation superalloy TMS-238 mainly results from Re and Ru additions []. Refractory alloys also play significant roles in industry. In the second generation nuclear power plants, the most-used materials for fuel cladding are Zircoloy 2 and Zircoloy 4. The Niobium alloy C103 is used for the nozzle extension of satellites [].
